title: Telling a story
topic: organizing a story in the past; time connectors
why: The last step of the unit on memories: you combine the three past tenses in a real story, with the connectors that give it rhythm (un día, de repente, mientras, al cabo de un rato, por fin, al final). You also learn to react when someone tells you a story (¡No me digas!, ¿Y qué pasó?, ¡Qué fuerte!), which is essential in a conversation in Spain.

{"lessons": ["

Words for telling a story

A good story is a series of well-linked events. These little words organize your story in time; most of them have a direct English equivalent.

SpanishEnglishExample
un díaone dayUn día fuimos de excursión a la sierra.
de repentesuddenly, all of a suddenDe repente empezó a llover.
entoncesthen, soEntonces llamamos a un taxi.
mientraswhileMientras esperábamos, hablamos con una señora.
al cabo de un ratoafter a whileAl cabo de un rato llegó el autobús.
por finat last (what a relief!)Por fin encontramos el hotel.
al finalin the endAl final fue un viaje estupendo.
al día siguientethe next dayAl día siguiente volvimos a casa.

Two pairs to keep apart

  • English “finally” covers two Spanish expressions. Por fin expresses relief after a wait: “at last!”. Al final simply says how the story ends: “in the end”.
  • Mientras introduces an action that lasts, so it's usually in the imperfect (mientras esperaba, while I was waiting). De repente introduces a sudden event, so it's in the indefinido (de repente sonó el móvil).

“The next day” is al día siguiente; don't confuse it with pasado mañana (the day after tomorrow). And al cabo de works with any length of time: al cabo de dos horas, al cabo de una semana.

", "

Three past tenses in one story

To tell an anecdote, you combine the three tenses you know. Each one has its role:

  • the imperfecto sets the scene: the weather, the place, what was going on;
  • the indefinido moves the story forward: the actions, the events;
  • the perfecto connects the story to today: a comment, a consequence for this year or this week.
Un día de agosto íbamos en coche por Galicia. Hacía calor y estábamos perdidos. De repente vimos a un señor en la carretera y paramos el coche. Al final nos invitó a comer en su casa. Este año hemos vuelto a su pueblo y hemos comido otra vez con él.One day in August we were driving through Galicia. It was hot and we were lost. Suddenly we saw a man on the road and stopped the car. In the end he invited us to lunch at his house. This year we've gone back to his village and had lunch with him again.
VerbTenseRole
íbamos, hacía, estábamosimperfectothe background
vimos, paramos, invitóindefinidothe events
hemos vuelto (este año)perfectothe link with today

The perfecto only appears if you come back to the present, with a time marker like este año or esta semana. A story that's over and done with, with no link to today, is told only with the imperfect and the indefinido.

", "

Reacting to a story

When someone tells you an anecdote in Spain, people react a lot, and out loud! These little phrases show you're listening and keep the story going.

ReactionMeaningRegister
¿Y qué pasó?And what happened?everyday
¿Y entonces?And then?everyday
¿En serio?Really? Seriously?everyday
¡No me digas!No way! You don't say!everyday
¡Qué fuerte!That's crazy! Wow!informal (Spain)
¡Qué miedo!How scary!everyday
¡Qué suerte!How lucky!everyday
¡Qué mala suerte!What bad luck!everyday
¡Menos mal!Thank goodness! Phew!everyday

¡No me digas! is a set phrase: grammatically, it's a negative command (“don't tell me”), a form you'll study later. For now, just learn it as it is.

— Y de repente el coche se paró en medio de la carretera. — ¡No me digas! ¿Y qué pasó?— And suddenly the car stopped in the middle of the road. — No way! And what happened?

¡Qué fuerte! is very common among young Spaniards, but it's informal: avoid it with your doctor or in a formal work situation. ¡Menos mal!, on the other hand, works everywhere.
